claims.claim: Float glass is made by floating molten glass on a bath of molten tin, which gives the sheet uniform thickness and a very flat surface, eliminating grinding.
claims.episode_span: By floating the molten glass on a bath of molten tin, the grinding step disappeared entirely rather than being refined.
claims.supporting_quote: made by floating molten glass on a bed of molten metal of a low melting point , typically tin

claims.claim: Alastair Pilkington (with Kenneth Bickerstaff) of Pilkington Brothers developed the float glass process between 1953 and 1957 at St Helens.
claims.episode_span: Alastair Pilkington at Pilkington Brothers looked past incremental improvements to the grinders and instead asked what the physics of a liquid already supplied
claims.supporting_quote: Between 1953 and 1957, at the Cowley Hill Works St Helens, Lancashire, Sir Alastair Pilkington and Kenneth Bickerstaff of the UK's Pilkington Brothers developed the first successful commercial application for forming a continuous ribbon of glass using a molten tin bath

claims.claim: Before float glass, plate glass was cast and then mechanically ground and polished on both faces, a costly process.
claims.episode_span: making a sheet of window glass meant pouring molten material, letting it cool into a rough plate, and then spending days or weeks grinding and polishing both faces
claims.supporting_quote: Before the development of float glass, larger sheets of plate glass were made by casting a large puddle of glass on an iron surface, and then polishing both sides, a costly process.

claims.claim: Molten tin suits the float process because it is denser than glass (so the glass floats) and has a low melting point.
claims.episode_span: Molten tin satisfied those conditions: its melting point is low, its density keeps the glass afloat without mixing, and its surface remains mirror-flat.
claims.supporting_quote: Molten tin is suitable for the float glass process because it has a higher density than glass, so the molten glass floats on it.

claims.claim: The tin bath is kept under a protective nitrogen-and-hydrogen atmosphere to prevent the tin from oxidizing.
claims.episode_span: both concerns were addressed by maintaining a slightly reducing atmosphere of nitrogen and hydrogen that prevented oxidation while keeping the two liquids from alloying at the interface
claims.supporting_quote: To prevent oxidation, the tin bath is provided with a positive pressure protective atmosphere of nitrogen and hydrogen

claims.claim: Pilkington spent seven years perfecting the float glass process before commercially successful manufacture.
claims.episode_span: Seven years of iterative redesign followed, during which the company continued to lose money on the pilot line.
claims.supporting_quote: spent seven years perfecting and patenting its commercially successful manufacture

claims.claim: Glass ribbon thickness in the float process is controlled by varying flow and draw (roller) speed.
claims.episode_span: why thickness could be varied within limits by changing draw speed and bath temperature
claims.supporting_quote: Variation in the flow speed and roller speed enables glass sheets of varying thickness to be formed.

claims.claim: Tin melts at 231.9 °C (505 K) and has a density of 7.287 g/cm3 -- a low melting point and a density well above that of glass.
claims.episode_span: Molten tin satisfied those conditions: its melting point is low, its density keeps the glass afloat without mixing
claims.source_title: Tin - Element information, properties and uses | Periodic Table (Royal Society of Chemistry)
claims.supporting_quote: Melting point 231.928°C, 449.47°F, 505.078 K Period 5 Boiling point 2586°C, 4687°F, 2859 K

claims.claim: Alastair Pilkington and Kenneth Bickerstaff invented the float glass process between 1953 and 1957, floating molten glass on a bath of molten tin to avoid the costly grinding and polishing of plate glass; Pilkington then licensed the process to manufacturers worldwide.
claims.episode_span: Alastair Pilkington at Pilkington Brothers looked past incremental improvements to the grinders and instead asked what the physics of a liquid already supplied
claims.supporting_quote: Between 1953 and 1957 Alastair Pilkington and Kenneth Bickerstaff invented the Float Glass Process, a revolutionary method of high quality flat glass production by floating molten glass over a bath of molten tin, avoiding the costly need to grind and polish plate glass to make it clear.

claims.claim: Pilkington Brothers became the sole British manufacturer of plate glass in 1903, and in the 1950s its employees Alastair Pilkington and Kenneth Bickerstaff invented the float process, which the firm licensed to other manufacturers for royalties.
claims.episode_span: Alastair Pilkington at Pilkington Brothers looked past incremental improvements to the grinders and instead asked what the physics of a liquid already supplied
claims.supporting_quote: During the 1950s, Pilkington employees Alastair Pilkington (no relation) and Kenneth Bickerstaff invented the float glass process; the firm leveraged licensing agreements for many other manufacturers to use this new process in exchange for royalty payments .

claims.claim: Most flat glass today is soda-lime glass made by the float process, which has been the main production route since the 1950s; plate polishing was one of the earlier methods it displaced.
claims.episode_span: Float glass lines now produce continuous ribbons kilometers long at thicknesses suitable for architectural and automotive use
claims.supporting_quote: Most flat glass is soda–lime glass , mainly produced by the float glass process since the 1950s.

claims.claim: Soda-lime (window) glass has a density of about 2.52 g/cm3 at 20 °C -- roughly a third of molten tin's -- which is why the glass ribbon floats on the tin bath.
claims.episode_span: its density keeps the glass afloat without mixing, and its surface remains mirror-flat
